subject: Coffee & Tea
title: How the Bean Changes Physically
description: A quick win: understand How the Bean Changes Physically.

hook.text: A coffee bean nearly doubles in size during roasting—expanding like popcorn as internal pressure builds.

buildup.text: Water inside the bean turns to steam. CO₂ forms from chemical reactions. Both gases push the bean's cell walls outward.

discovery.text: The bean loses 12–20% of its weight (mainly water and CO₂) but gains 50–100% in volume. It becomes porous and brittle.

twist.text: Darker roasts weigh less per bean—so a 'bag of dark roast' has fewer beans than the same weight in light roast.

climax.text: The physical transformation is so dramatic that roasted coffee is technically a different material than the green seed.

punchline.text: Bigger, lighter, porous, fragile. Heat rewrites the bean's entire structure.

quiz.question: What happens to a coffee bean's size during roasting?
options: It nearly doubles in size as internal gases expand

details.summary: During roasting the coffee bean nearly doubles in size, loses 12 to 20 percent of its weight in water and gas, shifts from green to brown, and changes from dense and tough to porous and brittle. These physical changes mirror the chemical transformations happening inside.
details.whyItMatters: Visual and physical cues help roasters monitor progress without relying solely on instruments. Recognizing these changes builds roasting intuition.
takeaways: Beans nearly double in volume due to internal gas expansion
Weight drops 12 to 20 percent as moisture and CO2 escape
The structure changes from dense and hard to porous and brittle

faq.question: Why do darker roasted beans weigh less than lighter ones?
faq.answer: Darker roasts lose more moisture and volatile compounds during the extended roasting time. This greater weight loss means you get fewer grams of roasted coffee from the same amount of green beans.

faq.question: How does the expansion of the bean affect grinding and brewing?
faq.answer: More porous, expanded beans grind more easily and extract faster during brewing. This is why dark roasts typically need a coarser grind or shorter brew time to avoid over-extraction.
